title: Structured output pipelines, fallbacks & runtime orchestration - demo w/ Vela Systems
summary: Redwood AE+SE walked Vela Systems through a structured-output and tool-calling demo: JSON mode with typed schemas, runtime fallbacks (model variants + region routing), and Console/Optimize recommendations for batching/caching. Security and pilot logistics discussed (VPC, KMS, SOC2). Agreed next step: run a 2-week bench with sample prompts; Redwood to share security packet and sample schema repo.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-08
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 53 minutes
Attendees: Alex Moreno (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (CTO - Vela), Maya Thompson (Lead ML Eng), Leo Rivera (Platform), Sophie Chen (Security)

--- Auto-generated Summary (optional) ---
Alex: quick demo of JSON mode and how we do guardrails + runtime fallbacks, show console and Optimize recs

[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): okay hi everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex, I'm the AE on the account. With me is Priya, our solutions engineer. quick round: Daniel, Maya, Leo?
[00:12] Daniel (Vela): Hey Alex, thanks. Daniel here. We'll be looking at structured responses for our customer-facing assistant, and how tool calls can be reliable in high throughput scenarios.
[00:23] Maya: yeah hi, Maya. mostly concerned about output correctness and being able to enforce data contracts.
[00:28] Priya (Redwood SE): great, we'll focus the demo there. we'll show JSON mode with typed schemas, then function/tool calling and fallback orchestration if latency or capacity changes.
[00:36] Leo: and Sophie from security will chime in on VPC/KMS stuff.
[00:40] Sophie (Security): yep, I'll ask the security questions as we go.

[02:05] Alex: ok starting the screen, this is Redwood Console, top left - API keys, models, routes. quick note - the JSON mode is exposed in both API and the Console playground so you get the same semantics across hosted and private.
[02:42] Priya: first slide - typed output. you define a JSON schema for the expected object. the model is constrained to that shape, and we validate on the agent side so you get deterministic keys. small caveat, of course there's still hallucination risk so we show fallback and validation hooks.
[03:15] Daniel: when you say validate on the agent side, is that before it gets to our downstream systems? we want zero bad payloads.
[03:26] Priya: yes, the runtime performs schema validation. if it fails, you can configure a few policies: drop, return an error with correction suggestions, or automatically call a repair tool to re-run the generation with a more constrained prompt.
[03:40] Maya: repair tool - is that a separate microservice? how do you orchestrate it?
[03:47] Priya: good q. the tool-calling flow is first-class: you register tool endpoints (webhook or internal function). The runtime will call the tool if the JSON validator returns failure, or as part of the primary response when you instruct the model to call a tool. We surface orchestration policies in Console: canary, fallback to cheaper model, route by region, etc.

[05:10] Alex: demo time. I'll run a sample prompt that should produce a structured invoice object (customer, line_items, totals). starting now.
[05:25] [Priya types, model streaming begins]
[05:40] Model: {"invoice_id":"INV-2432","customer":{"name":"Acme Co","email":"billing@acme.co"},"lines":[{"desc":"SaaS subscription","qty":1,"unit_price":500}],"tax":45,"total":545}
[06:02] Maya: looks clean. if the model returned strings for numbers would Redwood coerce? we need strict typing.
[06:12] Priya: yes we can coerce and also reject. in console you pick the enforcement level per route. we also add telemetry so you see rejection rates.

[07:30] Alex: next is function/tool calling. i'm going to show a payments tool registered as a webhook. model says "call payments.process(payload)" then runtime does the call, records the response, and returns a unified object.
[07:52] Model (stream): {"action":"payments.process","payload":{"invoice_id":"INV-2432","amount":545}}
[08:05] [Runtime calls payments webhook -> 200 OK]
[08:18] Model/Runtime: {"status":"processed","txn_id":"TXN-7890","processor":"stripe-prod"}
[08:30] Daniel: nice. what if the webhook times out? we don't want the user waiting.
[08:37] Priya: we have timeout and fallback policies. Options: retry with backoff, return best-effort partial result, or queue the action for async processing and return an acknowledgement. those policies are configured per tool.

[10:00] Maya: about fallback models - say we run into capacity, how do you ensure quality drops are acceptable?
[10:12] Priya: you define fallback chains and acceptability thresholds. in the console we show model performance profiles for latency and quality based on our evals. you can pin threshold metrics (p95 latency, and a quality score from your eval prompts). if a fallback would breach quality threshold, it won't be used.
[11:01] Leo: can fallback include routing to dedicated capacity in another region? we have regional compliance constraints.
[11:10] Alex: yes routing by region or tier is supported. smart routing rules let you route based on customer, route path, or SLOs. we also support automatic fallback to dedicated pools when hosted capacity is constrained - but that typically pairs with a contractual reserved capacity.

[13:00] Sophie (Security): quick security checklist questions: do you support VPC peering, customer-managed KMS, and SOC2 Type II?
[13:10] Alex: yes to all. Private deployments support VPC and on-prem. KMS/HSM integrations available; we reference the same in the security packet i'll send. hosted customers get tenant isolation and encryption at rest but for full control we recommend Redwood Private.
[13:32] Sophie: log retention and audit logs? we need records of tool invocations for compliance.
[13:38] Priya: full audit logs per request, including tool calls, inputs/outputs (configurable retention). Console exposes tracing and token-level cost breakdowns.

[15:20] [21:00 - skipped filler; conversation about pricing buckets and pilot sizing]
[21:05] Alex: on Optimize, we ran a few suggestions for the invoice workflow. it recommended prefix caching for repeated customer metadata, a small batch size for our latency profile, and int8 quantization for the encoder in the cheaper variant.
[21:25] Maya: are those recommendations automatically applied or suggested? we prefer to review.
[21:31] Priya: suggestions only. engineer approves changes. you can run a simulation in Console to estimate cost delta.

[24:00] Daniel: about observability - can we get token-level cost per route exported to our billing system?
[24:10] Alex: yes, we have a billing API plus CSV exports and webhooks. token-level breakdown per route, per model, per customer.

[26:40] [transcription artifact: speaker label glitch, Speaker 1 repeats phrase]
[26:45] Speaker 1: and what's the KB cache, sorry i mean KV cash--
[26:50] Priya: KV cache, yeah. sorry transcription. KV cache stores prefix key-values for faster generation on repeated contexts. we can persist it per customer or per route.

[29:00] Maya: let's talk about schema evolution. our invoice schema will change quarterly. how do you handle compatibility?
[29:12] Priya: Console has schema versioning. you can roll out new schema as canary and map old->new when possible. we also support JSON path migrations and a compatibility checker.

[31:50] Daniel: what about test harness? we need to run a 2-week bench with 10k queries to validate p95 and quality.
[32:05] Alex: we can co-run a pilot: you give us canonical prompts and evaluation scripts, we run them against hosted and dedicated variants, and provide a results spreadsheet with latency and quality regressions flagged.

[34:20] Leo: network-wise for Private, what's required? we'll need a peering CIDR and KMS key exchange.
[34:28] Alex: we'll attach the checklist in the packet. typical items: peering CIDR, allowed outbound rules for tooling, and KMS public key fingerprint.

[36:00] Sophie: is SSO SAML or OIDC supported for RBAC?
[36:07] Priya: both SAML and OIDC. plus SCIM for provisioning. RBAC is route and team-level.

[38:45] [demo continues: show console traces for a failing JSON validation and automated repair tool invocation]
[38:55] Priya: here you can see the validation error, we call the repair tool with context and the corrected payload gets written to the audit log.
[39:12] Maya: can the repair be prevented from auto-submitting to downstream systems? we want to gate it.
[39:20] Priya: yes, you can set the policy to require manual approval before a tool result is forwarded. that sits in the pipeline settings.

[41:00] Alex: pricing note - hosted is usage-based. dedicated has reserved capacity. for pilots we usually do a small reserved seat or credit. I'll follow up with numbers.

[43:30] Daniel: any showstoppers for us? major concerns are correctness, throughput, and SOC2.
[43:40] Alex: no showstoppers. the pilot will validate throughput and quality. we'll include SOC2 docs and an NDA if needed.

[45:10] Maya: a small nit: model outputs sometimes include slightly different key order; will that break our downstream parsers?
[45:20] Priya: we normalize ordering on the runtime — keys are canonicalized before validation so parsers see stable shapes.

[47:00] Sophie: last security Q -- are tool payloads logged in plain text? we need PII redaction options.
[47:08] Priya: logs can be redacted at ingestion via regex or structured filters; you can also configure non-persistent logging for particular routes.

[49:30] Alex: quick recap of next steps: we'll send security packet, demo artifacts (console recording and schema repo), and propose pilot start window.
[49:45] Daniel: good. we'll prepare prompt set and SLOs.

[50:20] Alex: any other items?
[50:30] Leo: just to confirm — who owns the benchmark run? Alex or Priya?
[50:35] Alex: Priya will run the bench with you; i'll coordinate contracting.

[51:10] Priya: thanks everyone. wrapping up. recording will be shared.
[51:25] [meeting ends]
